children.note: Two Houses, what Parliament is for, and the separate jobs of the National Assembly and the Senate.
Kenya's Parliament has two Houses, the National Assembly and the Senate, each doing the work this Constitution gives it.

manas.q: What two Houses make up Parliament (Article 93)?

children.note: Law-making power comes from the people and, nationally, belongs to Parliament, which may also amend the Constitution and change county boundaries as the Constitution allows. Nobody else may make binding law unless the Constitution or an Act gives them that power, and such an Act must spell out its purpose and limits.
Parliament reflects the nation's diversity, speaks for the people's will, guards the Constitution and promotes democracy.
Ministers and agencies make regulations only when an Act lets them, and that Act must state the purpose, limits, scope and standards of the power.

manas.q: Under Article 94(6), what must an Act that delegates law-making power state?

children.note: Regulations under a health Act (like tobacco rules) are valid only within what the Act allows. See BAT v CS Health in Chapter 2.

children.topic: Art. 95 · Role of the National Assembly
children.note: The National Assembly represents constituencies and special interests, debates the people's concerns and makes laws. It controls the national budget, oversees State organs, can start the removal of the President and other State officers, and approves war and longer emergencies.
Divides revenue between national and county levels, appropriates national spending, oversees national revenue.

manas.q: Which House appropriates money for the national government?

children.note: Checks how State officers, the President and Deputy included, behave in office, starts any removal, and oversees State organs.
Must approve any declaration of war, and any extension of a state of emergency.

The Senate represents the counties and protects their interests and governments. It makes laws that concern counties, divides revenue among the 47 counties and oversees it, and decides any impeachment of the President or Deputy President.
Considers, debates and approves Bills concerning counties (Articles 109–113).
Shares national revenue among counties (Article 217) and oversees what counties receive.

manas.q: Which House decides how revenue is shared among the counties?

children.note: The National Assembly accuses; the Senate tries and decides (Article 145).

manas.q: In removing a President, which House accuses and which decides?

children.note: Who sits in each House, who may be elected, election day, term, losing a seat, recall, membership disputes.

children.topic: Art. 97 · Who sits in the National Assembly
children.note: The National Assembly has 290 constituency members, 47 county women members, 12 members nominated by parties for special interests, and the Speaker as an ex officio member.
290 + 47 + 12 = 349 members, plus the Speaker.

manas.q: How many members does the National Assembly have, apart from the Speaker?

children.note: The 12 nominated seats are for groups such as youth, persons with disabilities and workers, shared by party strength (Article 90).
Women may still contest the 290 constituency seats; nothing reserves those for men.

children.topic: Art. 98 · Who sits in the Senate
children.note: The Senate has 47 elected senators, one per county, plus 16 women nominated by parties, a young man and a young woman, a man and a woman with disabilities, and the Speaker ex officio.
47 + 16 + 2 + 2 = 67 members, plus the Speaker.

manas.q: How many members does the Senate have, apart from the Speaker?

children.note: The 47 are elected county-wide; the other 20 come from party lists under Article 90.

children.topic: Art. 99 · Who can be elected an MP
children.note: A candidate must be a registered voter, meet any education, moral and ethical tests, and be nominated by a party or backed as an independent by enough voters. Public officers, recent IEBC members, county assembly members, people citizens for under ten years, bankrupts, those serving six months or more in prison and those found to have breached Chapter 6 are disqualified.
Registered voter; meets education, moral and ethical requirements; party nominee, or independent backed by 1,000 voters (National Assembly) or 2,000 (Senate).

manas.q: How many supporting voters does an independent need for the National Assembly and for the Senate?

children.note: Eight grounds.

manas.q: Name four grounds that disqualify a person from election to Parliament (Article 99(2)).

children.note: Any State or public officer other than an MP.
Within the previous five years.
Citizenship must go back at least ten years.
Cannot sit in both.
As found by law.
Until discharged.
Serving such a sentence at registration or on election day.
Found under a law to have abused office or broken the integrity rules.
A sentence or finding disqualifies only after every appeal or review is exhausted.
Parliament must pass laws that promote the presence in Parliament of women, persons with disabilities, youth, ethnic and other minorities, and marginalised communities.
This is the duty the Supreme Court relied on in 2012 when it set 27 August 2015 for measures on the two-thirds rule (see Chapter 7 cases).

manas.q: Which five groups does Article 100 want better represented?

children.note: General elections fall on the second Tuesday of August, once every five years. Vacant elected seats go to a by-election within 90 days and party-list seats are refilled within 21 days, but no vacancy is filled in the last three months before a general election.
Second Tuesday in August, every five years. 9 August 2022 was one; the next falls in August 2027.

manas.q: On what day is a general election held under Article 101?

children.note: Speaker notifies the IEBC within 21 days; by-election within 90 days of the vacancy.
Speaker notifies the IEBC and the party within 21 days; filled as an Act says within 21 days of notice.
No by-election or refill in the three months before a general election.
Each House sits until the next general election day. Only when Kenya is at war may two-thirds of each House extend it, six months at a time and twelve months in total.
At war only; two-thirds of all members of each House; at most 6 months per extension and 12 months overall.

manas.q: When and for how long may Parliament's term be extended?

children.topic: Art. 103 · When an MP loses the seat
children.note: A seat falls vacant on death, resignation, removal under the Constitution or a Chapter 6 law, the end of the term, a later disqualification, or missing eight sittings in a session without the Speaker's written leave or a good reason. It also falls vacant if a party member leaves the party, or an independent joins one.
Absent from eight sittings in one session without written permission and without an explanation the committee accepts.

manas.q: How many unexcused absences cost an MP the seat?

children.note: Elected on a party ticket and you resign (or are deemed to resign) from it: seat lost. Elected independent and you join a party: seat lost. An Act says when someone is "deemed" to have resigned.
Changing parties mid-term is not free: the seat itself is lost, and a by-election follows (Article 101(4)).
Voters may recall their MP or senator before the term ends, on grounds and by a procedure that Parliament sets in law.
The recall grounds and procedure are set by statute (the Elections Act). Check the current position on new.kenyalaw.org (checked 27 Nov 2026).

manas.q: Who sets the grounds and procedure for recalling an MP?

children.note: The High Court decides whether a person was validly elected to Parliament and whether a seat has become vacant, and must do so within six months of the petition.
The time limit for the High Court to finish such a petition.

manas.q: Which court decides if an MP was validly elected, and within what time?

children.note: Speakers, who presides, majority and minority leaders.

Each House elects a Speaker from people qualified to be MPs but who are not MPs, and a Deputy Speaker from its own members. The offices end when a new House first sits, on resignation, on the holder leaving Parliament, or by a two-thirds vote.
Eligible to be an MP but not currently one.

manas.q: Must the Speaker be a sitting member of the House?

children.note: A resolution with the votes of two-thirds or more of the House's members.
The Speaker presides, then the Deputy Speaker, then a member the House elects. At a joint sitting the National Assembly Speaker presides with the Senate Speaker assisting.

manas.q: Who presides over a joint sitting of the two Houses?

children.note: The leader of the largest party or coalition in the National Assembly is the majority leader, and of the second largest the minority leader. In the Assembly the order of precedence is Speaker, majority leader, minority leader.

manas.q: How are the majority and minority leaders identified (Article 108)?

children.note: How Bills pass, county Bills (special and ordinary), mediation, money Bills, presidential assent, when Acts start.

Parliament legislates through Bills it passes and the President signs. Bills not about counties go only through the National Assembly, county Bills go through both Houses, and money Bills start only in the National Assembly.
Any member or committee of the House concerned.
Ordinary national Bill: National Assembly only. County Bill: either House first, then the other. Money Bill: National Assembly only.

manas.q: Which House must a money Bill start in?

children.note: A county Bill is one about county functions in the Fourth Schedule, county elections, or county finances under Chapter 12. Election Bills and the yearly County Allocation of Revenue Bill are "special"; the rest are "ordinary", and the two Speakers decide jointly which a Bill is.
Special: county assembly or executive elections, and the County Allocation of Revenue Bill (Article 218). Ordinary: every other county Bill.

manas.q: Name the two kinds of special Bill concerning counties.

children.note: Before debate, both Speakers settle together whether it concerns counties and, if so, which kind.
Once both Houses pass it in the same form, the originating Speaker sends it to the President within seven days.

A special Bill follows the ordinary route, but once the Senate passes it the National Assembly can amend or veto it only by a two-thirds vote. If that vote fails, the Senate's version goes to the President within seven days.

manas.q: What vote does the National Assembly need to amend or veto a special Bill passed by the Senate?

children.note: If the second House rejects an ordinary county Bill it goes to mediation; if it amends it, the first House reconsiders. If the first House accepts the amendments the Bill goes to the President, and if it rejects them, to mediation.
House A passes → House B passes (done), amends (back to A) or rejects (mediation) → A agrees (to President) or disagrees (mediation).
The two Speakers appoint an equal number of members from each House to agree a version both can pass. If they fail within 30 days, or either House rejects their version, the Bill dies.
The committee's deadline to agree a version.

manas.q: What happens if a mediation committee cannot agree within 30 days?

children.note: The National Assembly Speaker passes it on for the President's signature within a week.

A money Bill deals only with taxes, charges on public funds, public money, government loans and matters incidental to them, and a money Bill may cover nothing else. On such matters the National Assembly acts on its committee's recommendation after hearing the Treasury Cabinet Secretary.

Taxes; charges on a public fund; appropriating, receiving, keeping, investing or issuing public money; raising, guaranteeing or repaying loans; incidental matters. County taxes and loans are excluded, and so is the Article 218 revenue Bill.

manas.q: List three subjects that make a Bill a "money Bill".

children.note: A Finance Bill that changes tax rates is a money Bill and starts in the National Assembly.

Within 14 days the President must sign a Bill or send it back with reservations. Parliament may then amend it to meet them, or pass it again by two-thirds, after which the President must sign within seven days; if the President does nothing in time, the Bill counts as signed.
The President's time to sign or refer back.

manas.q: How long does the President have to assent to or refer back a Bill?

children.note: Two-thirds of National Assembly members, and two-thirds of Senate delegations if the Senate must approve the Bill.

manas.q: What vote does Parliament need to pass a Bill over the President's reservations?

children.note: Silence past the deadline is treated as assent.

An Act is published in the Gazette within seven days of assent and takes effect 14 days later unless it names another date. An Act giving MPs a direct financial benefit starts only after the next general election.
A pay rise for MPs cannot benefit the Parliament that passed it; it waits until after the next election. Benefits MPs share as ordinary members of the public are not caught.

manas.q: When does an Act giving MPs a direct financial benefit come into force?

children.note: Assent on 1 March, Gazette on 5 March, no start date stated: the Act takes effect on 19 March.
Free speech, openness, petitions, languages, quorum, voting, Senate delegations, committees, summoning witnesses.

children.topic: Art. 117 · Freedom of speech in Parliament
children.note: Members may speak and debate freely in Parliament, and Parliament may set out by law the powers, privileges and immunities of its Houses, committees, leaders and members.
Parliamentary Powers and Privileges Act 2017. Check the current version on new.kenyalaw.org (checked 27 Nov 2026).

manas.q: What freedom does Article 117 guarantee in Parliament?

children.topic: Art. 118 · Open Parliament and public participation
children.note: Parliament and its committees sit in public and must help people take part in law-making. The public or media may be shut out only in exceptional cases the Speaker justifies.
Real public participation is a test courts apply to laws and regulations; see Article 10 and BAT v CS Health in Chapter 2.

manas.q: Under Article 118, when may Parliament exclude the public?

children.note: Anyone may petition Parliament on any matter within its power, including asking it to make, change or repeal a law, following procedures Parliament sets.

manas.q: Who may petition Parliament under Article 119, and about what?

children.note: Parliament works in Kiswahili, English and Kenyan Sign Language. If language versions of an Act conflict, the version the President signed wins.

manas.q: Which version of an Act prevails if its language versions conflict?

children.note: The National Assembly needs 50 members present to do business, and the Senate 15.

manas.q: What is the quorum of the National Assembly and of the Senate?

children.note: Unless the Constitution says otherwise, questions are decided by a majority of members present and voting; the Speaker has no vote and a tie means the motion fails. Members may not vote where they have a financial interest.
Lost, because the Speaker cannot break it.

manas.q: What happens to a motion when the votes are tied?

children.note: When counting members for a vote, the Speaker is left out.

Senators registered in a county form one delegation led by the elected senator. On matters affecting counties each delegation casts one vote after consulting its members and a majority of all delegations is needed; on other matters each senator votes individually.
One vote per county, 47 in total; a matter passes only with 24 or more delegations in favour.

manas.q: On county matters in the Senate, who votes and how many votes are needed?

children.note: For anything other than a Bill, the Speaker rules whether it affects counties.

Each House may form committees and must make Standing Orders for its business, and the Houses may form joint committees. Approvals of appointments are first examined in public by a committee and then voted on by the House.
Appointments needing approval go to a committee, its recommendation is tabled, and both stages are public.

manas.q: How does Parliament handle an appointment that needs its approval?

children.note: Proceedings still stand despite a vacancy or the presence of someone not entitled to be there.
Each House and its committees may summon anyone to give evidence and have the High Court's powers to compel attendance, take oaths, demand documents and examine witnesses abroad.

manas.q: What court powers do parliamentary committees have under Article 125?

children.note: Where Parliament sits, the Parliamentary Service Commission, Clerks and staff.
A House may sit anywhere in Kenya at any time it chooses. After an election the President gazettes the place and date of the first sitting, within 30 days of the election.

manas.q: Within how many days of an election must a new House first sit?

children.note: The Commission runs Parliament's services, staff and budget and promotes parliamentary democracy. It is chaired by the National Assembly Speaker with seven MPs from government and opposition sides and two outside members, and the Clerk of the Senate is its secretary.

Speaker of the National Assembly (chair); a vice-chair chosen from the seven MPs; four MPs from the governing side (at least two women) and three from the others (at least one woman, at least one from each House); one man and one woman from outside Parliament.

manas.q: Who chairs the Parliamentary Service Commission?

children.note: Services and facilities for Parliament; creating and filling staff posts; preparing the parliamentary budget for the National Assembly; promoting parliamentary democracy; members' and staff welfare.
Each House has a Clerk, chosen by the Parliamentary Service Commission and approved by that House. The Clerks and their staff belong to the Parliamentary Service.

manas.q: Who appoints the Clerk of each House?
